svg.title: From a human connectome to its memory capacity
svg.desc: An animated explanation in fourteen scenes. The connectome is a network of 90 brain regions linked by nerve fibres, and every link has a weight. Disparity measures how evenly a region spreads its strength over its connections; subgraph centrality adds up the loops by which activity returns to a region; the stable rank counts the independent directions that carry the weight of the whole network. The connectome is then used as the fixed recurrent layer of a neural network: a random signal is fed into every region and a trained readout tries to recall the signal a number of steps back. Recall fades with the delay; this is the forgetting curve, and the area under it is the memory capacity. Two connectomes with different weights have different memory capacities. In the example the heaviest links join the two hemispheres, and halving those weights on the same wiring raises the memory capacity.

g.text: The connectome: the brain as a network
Disparity: how a region spreads its strength
Loops: activity leaves a region and comes back
Stable rank: the network’s independent directions
Now the connectome becomes a neural network
A random signal is fed into every region
Can its present state recall the past signal?
Recall fades with the delay: the forgetting curve
The area under it is the memory capacity
Its heaviest links join the two hemispheres
Halve them, same wiring: it remembers more
a few are strong, most are weak
back in two steps, in three, in four…
subgraph centrality adds up all the loops
each bar is one independent direction
its height, the weight it carries
Memory depends on the weights, not only on the wiring.
From birth to old age, it follows the weight between the hemispheres.
